item.title: Macron Dreamed of Reviving France, but His Term Is Ending in Crisis
item.description:
As thousands of high school students took to the streets last week in a collective cry of youthful anger, President Emmanuel Macron of France traveled to a navy ship off the coast of Brittany. From the deck, he watched the firing of a new ballistic missile from a French nuclear-powered submarine.

It was a telling display of Mr. Macron’s priorities in a country where the president, by tradition, rises above the messy scrum of domestic politics. Mr. Macron left it to his prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, to try to reassure the French people that the government was handling the proliferating unrest.

It also reflected how Mr. Macron, after nearly a decade in power, has failed to solve the manifold problems afflicting France’s economy and welfare system — problems he promised to address when he was elected in 2017, at 39, as an ambitious reformer, and which have now coalesced into a systemic crisis.

“Remember, Macron published a book before the 2017 election, called ‘Révolution,’” said Jérôme Fourquet, a political analyst at the polling institute IFOP. “We told ourselves: he will relaunch the machine, he will lead a revolution.”

With just seven months before he leaves office, the president “hasn’t been able to bring about this revolution,” Mr. Fourquet said. Instead, the analyst said, he may be remembered as “the last captain of the boat.”

On Tuesday, thousands of students were set again to protest overcrowded classrooms, dilapidated school buildings and a shortage of teachers. The protests, now in their fourth week, added to the portrait of a country in disarray.

So dire are France’s fiscal problems that experts say the country may finally be forced to reckon with the foundering of its generous welfare state. Such a scenario could trigger painful cuts to benefits or even a default on France’s debt.

To be sure, many of these problems predated Mr. Macron. Some were exacerbated by events out of his control, like the coronavirus pandemic and wars in Iran and Ukraine, which fueled inflation and further busted the budget.

Still, critics say Mr. Macron failed to make a dent in France’s longstanding structural problems, either because of public blowback or his own political miscalculations. His legacy, then, is likely to be one of unfulfilled promise.

Mr. Macron’s office declined to comment.

A onetime investment banker who had served as economics minister, Mr. Macron came in promising to revitalize France’s economy by cutting taxes on businesses and high-income people, loosening labor laws and overhauling the pension system. This, he said, would nurture an entrepreneurial culture and make France attractive again to investors, which would reignite economic growth.

Mr. Macron accomplished the first two goals but not the third. He set off angry protests after pushing through an unpopular rise in France’s retirement age to 64 from 62, a move that economists say was critical to stemming the tide of red ink. After Mr. Macron lost his majority in the National Assembly, lawmakers bowed to popular sentiment, voting in 2025 to pause the change.

At the same time, Mr. Macron’s elimination of a tax on wealthy people earned him the unflattering sobriquet “president of the rich.” That became a political problem as rising prices created a cost-of-living squeeze. From 2018 to 2020, France was convulsed by the “Yellow Vest” protest movement, which began when people turned out to demonstrate against fuel prices and a litany of other grievances.

“We never had so many very rich people, and we have many people who can’t make ends meet,” said Jean-Yves Camus, a political scientist at the Jean Jaurès Foundation, a left-leaning think tank in Paris. “French society, which always aimed at being egalitarian, is going the American way.”

France, of course, remains starkly different to the United States when it comes to the size of the state. In 2025, public spending — on heath care, pensions, education, culture and other benefits — amounted to 57.3 percent of France’s total economic output. That is the second highest percentage in the European Union, after Finland’s, and more than 20 points higher than in the United States.

Total public debt is now projected to reach 120 percent of gross domestic product in 2027, the third-highest ratio after those of Greece and Italy.

Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and President Trump’s return to power in 2024, compounded France’s costs because it has had to spend more on its military — both to counter Russian threats and to rely less on America’s security umbrella.

Even critics credit Mr. Macron for leading calls for the continent to take on more responsibility for its security. His blueprint for “strategic autonomy” from the United States once seemed unrealistic, even grandiose. Given Mr. Trump’s disparagement of NATO, it now seems prescient.

“He has tried to build a global European vision,” said Gérard Araud, a former French ambassador to Washington, said of Mr. Macron, whom he has advised. “Whatever you think of it, he has been the voice of Europe.”

But Mr. Araud said that the qualities that had enabled Mr. Macron to stride the global stage have hurt him at home. His elite credentials and intellectual manner have made him seem out-of-touch in meat-and-potatoes France, he said.

“He’s the ultimate arugula president in a populist time,” said Mr. Araud, recalling an early episode in which Barack Obama, who some say shares a few of Mr. Macron’s highhanded traits, was tweaked for mentioning rarefied salad leaves in a meeting with farmers.

French voters have long since grown disillusioned with Mr. Macron. His approval rating stood at 15 percent, the lowest level since he took office, according to a poll last week by the polling firm, Ipsos. Mr. Macron’s eroding popularity has coincided with a skein of electoral setbacks, some of them self-inflicted.

After his party was badly beaten in European Parliament elections in 2024, the president called snap elections within France. The decision, which surprised his advisers, backfired, leaving his party with fewer seats in the national Parliament.

Mr. Macron found himself with little room for legislative maneuver as France’s fiscal situation continued to deteriorate. His push to overhaul the French state was by then a memory. The eruption of the Iran war drove up energy prices again, further clouding France’s economic picture.

Even in pushing for an end to the conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, Mr. Macron has found himself largely on the sidelines of negotiations dominated by the United States. One exception was when he recently negotiated a deal with Mr. Trump and other leaders to release 100 million barrels of stockpiled crude oil and diesel to ease prices that war has raised.

At home, Mr. Macron has cycled through prime ministers as the government has labored to pass a budget. The seemingly unending drama over France’s finances has deepened the doubts of investors about the country’s creditworthiness.

With yields on France’s bonds briefly crossing the dangerous threshold of 5 percent, there are fears that the country could tumble into a full-blown financial crisis. Investors are also alarmed by the prospect that the far-right leader Marine Le Pen has a plausible path to the presidency next spring.

Mr. Macron, who twice defeated Ms. Le Pen, has long presented himself as a bulwark against the far right. But his inability to turn his political movement into a self-sustaining centrist party, analysts said, has contributed to the withering of France’s political center, leaving the country vulnerable to a far-right takeover.

Alain Minc, a French businessman who was a close adviser to Mr. Macron before falling out with him midway through his tenure, said the president’s legacy could be divided neatly into halves.

Mr. Macron’s first term, during which he pushed through some significant changes, was “more than decent.” His second, Mr. Minc said, was a “drama,” culminating in the current crisis, which has prompted some to question whether France will need to be bailed out by the European Central Bank.

“His legacy will be dramatic,” Mr. Minc said, and not in a good way. “For France to need the support of the E.C.B. is the most humiliating position to be in.”

Giulia Imbert and Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting.

item.title: This Copper Mine Led to a Civil War. Can Reopening It Fund a New Nation?
item.description:
The years had covered the skeletal structures of the abandoned mine with rust, filling its shafts with sludge and debris several stories deep. Green leaves sprouted from crumbling industrial equipment. What was left of a water pump station was repurposed as a church, with steel beams for pews.

Four decades ago, the vast Panguna mine on Bougainville, an island on the eastern edge of Papua New Guinea, abruptly shut down. It closed after sabotage by residents irate that less than 2 percent of the wealth generated by the Australian-run copper and gold mine went to the local community, even though it obliterated whole villages and buried swaths of land downstream in mine waste.

That anger spiraled into a decade-long civil war in the island’s jungles, as a ragtag separatist militia held Papua New Guinea’s military at bay. “The Crisis,” as it is now known, left as many as 15,000 people dead and displaced a generation, while cementing Bougainville’s desires for independence.

Now, the dormant mine is whirring back to life, spurred by aspirations for the region to become the world’s newest country — and a growing appetite for copper. Its leader, President Ishmael Toroama, a former rebel commander, has pledged Bougainville will be governing itself by next year, its future funded by the mine.

Global demand for the estimated 5.3 million tons of copper buried in its depths has surged. But the rush of interest raises the question: Will its resources be extracted in a way that benefits the people of Bougainville, or will history repeat itself?

Late last year, the Autonomous Bougainville Government brought on a little-known Indian company, Lloyds Metals and Energy, as a partner in redeveloping the mine. Since then, heavy machinery has been careening along unpaved roads leading to the pit, while mining engineers and technicians from India have filled lodges in the nearby town of Arawa. Former combatants loyal to the president guard access to the mine, which Lloyds said in a statement should resume operations in early 2028.

The rapid progression has unnerved some landowners, observers and older Bougainvilleans who remember the descent into conflict and worry of renewed violence.

“If you’re walking fast, too fast, you have more chances of sliding over and probably you can even break your head,” said Dennis Kuiai, who fought alongside the president and is now a regional director in the Justice Department. “We should be taking time, making sure that we are doing things the right way.”

Lloyds said in the statement it was aware of the sensitivities.

“Panguna’s history makes careful consultation with landowners and communities essential,” the company said, adding that its aim was a project that “delivers lasting local benefits.”

Tensions briefly erupted this month, when 45 heavy vehicles bearing the Lloyds insignia were set on fire by saboteurs presumed to be local alluvial miners. Mr. Toroama called it an “isolated act of violence by individuals” and said work will “continue without delay.”

The geography around Panguna is defined by vestiges of the mine. Instead of referring to villages by name, people will say they live by the drainage tunnel, the water pump station, in the pit or on the upper, middle or lower tailings — large areas covered in mine waste.

In August, New York Times journalists spent several days in Bougainville, traveling to the bottom of the mine pit and throughout the area, speaking to residents and workers. In a sign of sensitivities, some workers accused journalists of spying for other would-be mine operators, and an agitated group of men who said they were former combatants briefly wrested away the photographer’s camera.

Philip Ken’s village, which was forced to relocate three times because of the mine, now sits by the pump station-turned-church. There, the psalm from Sunday’s service was scrawled on a chalkboard, and two statues of the Virgin Mary gazed out at the nave.

Born in 1970, two years before the mine opened, Mr. Ken only knows from stories what his home was like before — that wild pigs roamed, and the river teemed with fish. “My family was living downstream. Now it’s a desert,” said Mr. Ken, 56. He fought in the Bougainville Revolutionary Army in the conflict that lasted from 1988 to 1998. “I fought for my land, having heard what the mining had done.”

In the years since the mine was halted, people in his village and others have relied on panning for gold in the runoff. The tough but profitable work draws children as young as 10. Many use mercury because it binds to gold. The health effects are apparent in his community, where few live past 60, Mr. Ken said.

“You cannot see gray hairs in the tailings,” he said.

For the first time in decades, Lloyds is promising new jobs. Young women from Mr. Ken’s village are among 150 the company has started training to sew — but the wages pale in comparison with alluvial mining.

Whether Bougainville can be economically viable on its own has been a key question on its path to independence.

In a peace agreement signed in 2001, Papua New Guinea and Bougainville’s leaders agreed that the territory would be run autonomously, and that a referendum would be held to determine its political future. In 2019, that vote was finally held, and Bougainvilleans’ wishes were resounding: 98 percent wanted independence. At the same time, lawmakers in Papua New Guinea have questioned whether Bougainville can sustain itself economically.

Delivering independence has fallen to Mr. Toroama, the president, whose left arm was maimed by a grenade in the crisis. He has referred to the mine as the “economic guarantor for Bougainville’s independence” saying Panguna will free Bougainville from dependence on Papua New Guinea, which still funds most of its budget.

Not everyone is convinced.

“The president thinks we get independence just by opening the mine,” said Michael Pariu, 77, chief of the Nasioi people, whose village is near the tunnel. The rush to reopen seemed to take precedence over other basic preparations, like governance, social services and education, he said.

Mr. Toroama did not respond to multiple requests for an interview.

In November, Mr. Toroama surprised Bougainvilleans by signing a memorandum of understanding with Lloyds Metals, which operates iron ore mines in India but had no track record of developing or operating mines internationally. Mr. Toroama rejected a proposal to partner with CMOC, a major Chinese miner and one of the world’s top copper producers.

“If Lloyds Metals and Energy Limited truly respects Bougainville’s past, then the first test will be transparency, accountability, and a clear demonstration of how this partnership will uplift our people — not just extract our resources,” one resident, Walter Magut Buk, wrote in a Facebook comment on the day of the announcement.

The lack of transparency over the selection process has prompted concern about the company and its relationship to Mr. Toroama.

In February, John Momis, who served as president from 2010-2020, issued a statement questioning whether Lloyds had the ability to raise the billions necessary to reopen the mine.

He also criticized “a range of benefits and inducements” the company had provided Mr. Toroama, including flying his wife to India for “serious and expensive medical assistance.” In a community interwoven with family connections, it is widely known that the president’s wife was taken to India for a kidney transplant — a type of lifesaving care few in Bougainville have access to.

Lloyds said it provided assistance to Betty Toroama for “humanitarian” reasons.

“We reject the suggestion that our assistance was intended to influence the selection of a development partner for Panguna,” the company said.

By mid-August, signs of Lloyds’ ramp-up of operations were apparent throughout the Panguna area and in Arawa. Residents carried golf umbrellas bearing the Bougainville flag and the Lloyds logo, reinforcing the association between independence and the company. Rows of new heavy machinery sat in the nearby Loloho Port. Construction was in full swing at the site of a 100-bed hospital Lloyds had promised to build.

In a mine shaft inside the Panguna pit, workers said they had been shoveling away for a month at 40 years of accumulated sludge. One man said he was being paid minimum wage of 5 kina per an hour, about $1.12, and had not been given gloves or masks. He glanced over his shoulder, and stopped speaking when an Indian supervisor approached.

A former Lloyds employee, who asked not to be named because they have been threatened by former combatants, said the company did not sign employment contracts and made most payments in cash. The company said that although some early salaries may have been paid in cash, all current employees had contracts.

“We’d always be told, the president wants this done,” the former employee said. “We need to do this quickly, we want this yesterday.”

Lloyds promised that they can get the mine up and running faster than other companies, particularly Western ones, said Samson Kaissy, chairman of the landowners’ council.

“With Lloyds, they will never waste time. Once they talk, at the same time, they bring the funds,” he said.

The race to restart the mine complicates another hard-fought process: cleaning up the devastation left behind by the departure of Rio Tinto, the mine’s Australian former operator.

Theonila Roka Matbob was among 156 Bougainvilleans who filed a complaint against the mining giant in 2020, seeking remediation for environmental and human rights harms. Some of the most urgent work was getting underway just as Lloyds entered the picture, she said. Rio Tinto has said it is continuing to engage in efforts to address the mine’s impacts.

“We have a legacy to fix,” said Ms. Matbob, who filed the complaint with Australia’s Human Rights Law Center. She said she worried the hurried reopening was “jumping on the wagon on the way to more destruction.”

Ms. Matbob, 35, whose father was killed during the crisis, said her village had been rebuilding the community and rehabilitating their land. From 1972 to 1988, the mine was churning out 100,000 tons of waste rock daily, enough to fill a football field three stories high, deposited downstream.

On a rainy day in early August, in a bid to ease tensions, the government staged a “blood cleansing” ritual at the mine to release the land of its burdens. It said in a statement it wanted to dispel notions that former combatants were taking over mine operations by force.

Mr. Toroama, with an array of Lloyds umbrellas visible behind him, assured his people that everything was in service of Bougainville’s independence.

“This is it, the time is here with us,” he thundered, over the drumming of the downpour. “Together with Lloyds Metals, the work must progress.”

item.title: Pope Leo Prepares for Surgery to Remove Lung Nodule
item.description:
Pope Leo XIV will undergo surgery on Tuesday to remove a nodule from his lung, the Vatican said. It will be Leo’s first medical issue requiring hospitalization since he became the pontiff last year.

Leaving the Vatican on Tuesday morning, Leo waved through a rolled-down car window to a group of well-wishers that had gathered outside the Vatican walls.

He received a hero’s welcome when he arrived at the main entrance of the Policlinico A. Gemelli hospital, with dozens of people waving and cheering as the pontiff made his way inside.

“We’re with you,” one person called out from the crowd.

The Vatican said previously that Leo was expected to spend about a week recovering in the hospital after the surgery, and that all audiences with the pope were canceled until Oct. 20.

The pope, 71, announced during his weekly blessing and prayer in St. Peter’s Square on Sunday that doctors had advised the surgical intervention after detecting a “very early-stage and well-localized” nodule during recent medical tests.

Pulmonary nodules are very common, and most are benign, according to the American Lung Association.

Dr. Marco Alloisio, a thoracic surgeon at the Humanitas Cancer Center in Milan, emphasized that “a pulmonary nodule isn’t necessarily synonymous with lung cancer.”

He said that any further treatment would depend on the histological examination of the nodule and other biological tests that would check for genetic mutations. Dr. Alloisio, who is not part of the pope’s care, called it “very positive” that Leo had been receiving checkups.

Lung cancer remains the leading cause of cancer deaths in the United States, and older adults are at higher risk. Annual screening has been shown to save lives.

Dr. Lorenzo Spaggiari, a thoracic surgical oncologist at the European Institute of Oncology in Milan who is also not part of the pope’s medical team, said the pope’s surgery was likely to be minimally invasive, using robotic surgical procedures. A biopsy of the nodule would determine whether it needed to be removed and, if so, what percentage of the pulmonary lobe along with it.

While hospitalized, the pope is expected to remain in charge at the Vatican unless he is incapacitated, but day-to-day decisions are to be handled by its sprawling bureaucracy. Any major decision requiring papal approval is expected to be postponed until his release.

The pope had been scheduled to preside on Wednesday over the concluding Mass for a Vatican meeting about how a document on marriage and the family has been followed in the 10 years since it was issued.

Instead, the Mass will be presided over by Cardinal Luis Antonio Tagle, 69, who was approved by Leo last week as the new dean of the College of Cardinals. The dean, who coordinates the activities of his fellow cardinals, plays an important role during any papal transition.

However, Leo appeared optimistic that he would be on his feet soon. He is scheduled to travel to South America early next month, a homecoming of sorts given that he worked and lived in Peru for many years. In his remarks last Sunday, Leo suggested he was still planning to go.

Dr. Spaggiari said that after lung surgery, patients are advised not to travel by plane for three weeks.

Asked whether the trip, which is to begin on Nov. 6, was still on the pope’s schedule, Matteo Bruni, the Vatican spokesman, said Tuesday morning that the pope had said it was.

item.title: Ukraine Says It Received No Intelligence About Strikes 2 Nights in a Row
item.description:
Ukraine said it received no warning from its Western partners before a Russian missile attack against Kyiv on Tuesday night, after reporting earlier in the day that it had gotten no intelligence about a round of strikes the night before.

The news raised fears in Ukraine that the Trump administration had made good on apparent threats to cut off intelligence sharing that includes alerts of such attacks, even as both U.S. and Ukrainian officials asserted that intelligence continued to flow.

Before the latest Russian attack on Kyiv, President Trump said Tuesday that the United ⁠States was continuing to share intelligence with Ukraine. “We are helping them, and we are sharing intel,” he told reporters who had asked him about the possibility of cutting off intelligence if Kyiv did not halt strikes on Russian oil refineries.

The Ukrainian foreign minister also said on Tuesday that intelligence sharing was continuing, asserting that the attack the night before went undetected “because of a special type of weaponry which was used by the Russian side.”

Mr. Zelensky then weighed in again late on Tuesday, after the second ballistic missile attack. “Russian missile strike on Kyiv,” he wrote on social media. “Once again, no warning from our partners.”

He called the situation “absolutely unjust,” adding that Russia was “destroying our energy infrastructure, and Ukraine is not even receiving early warnings about ballistic missile launches.”

Commenting on the first attack, some military experts said there may have been no warning simply because it was not detected before launch, which has happened in the past, and not because of the United States withholding intelligence.

Russia has previously fired missiles that Western satellites have struggled to track, including S-400 missiles, which Ukraine has at times described as ballistic weapons. Serhiy Beskrestnov, a military expert who advises Mr. Zelensky, said after the attack on Monday that it was not the first time Western partners had failed to detect a launch of S-400 missiles.

Still, it would be unusual for Kyiv’s Western allies to fail to detect two missile attacks in a row.

Fears that Washington might cut off intelligence sharing with Ukraine emerged after Mr. Trump struck a deal with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia to buy millions of tons of Russian fuel. The agreement is part of an effort to bring down sky-high diesel prices, caused mostly by the U.S.-Israeli war against Iran, before the U.S. midterm elections.

As they presented the deal to the Ukrainians at a meeting last week in Miami, Trump administration officials asked Kyiv to stop striking Russian oil refineries so that Russian diesel could flow back onto the market. They said Kyiv owed Washington for critical U.S. intelligence assistance, which some in the room took as a veiled threat. A U.S. official later denied any suggestion that intelligence support would be withheld.

Mr. Zelensky said Ukraine had refrained from attacking Russian oil refineries over the past two days, framing it as a gesture of good will toward Mr. Trump, who on Friday declared an energy cease-fire that neither Kyiv nor Moscow has confirmed.

Ukraine has warned that such a cease-fire would work only if Russia stopped its attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities. Russia has continued to strike power plants even after Mr. Trump declared an energy cease-fire, Kyiv says. Mr. Zelensky said Tuesday night’s strike targeted a combined heat-and-power plant supplying Kyiv.

“The facts show that the Russians do not consider themselves bound by what the President of the United States said,” he wrote on social media. “Ukraine supported an energy cease-fire. Russia is targeting yet another power plant and the lives of our people.”

The Trump administration has shown before that it is willing to withhold intelligence as a lever against Ukraine. After a White House meeting in which Mr. Trump berated Mr. Zelensky in front of journalists in early 2025, Washington paused intelligence sharing with Ukraine for a few days.

On Monday, Russian missiles struck Kyiv around 10 p.m. local time. Air-raid alerts sounded too late, after the missiles had been launched, leaving residents with no warning. The lapse immediately prompted speculation online that Washington had halted intelligence sharing. Air-raid alerts sounded late, again, in the attack on Tuesday.

Ukraine lacks the extensive satellite-based intelligence capabilities of the United States and relies on information from Western partners to monitor Russian military preparations signaling an attack. That includes activity at air bases, movements of ships and the deployment of ballistic missile launchers.

“Our NATO partners inform us when there is activity involving strategic aviation. Flights from one airfield to another. Where missiles are being delivered,” Col. Yurii Ihnat, a Ukrainian Air Force spokesman, said in an interview this summer. Sometimes, he added, Western satellites detected a flash indicating a missile launch, and partners immediately informed Ukraine.

Commenting on the Monday attack, Colonel Ihnat told Ukrainian national television that Western intelligence sometimes “fails to arrive.”

“This is not the first case,” he said. “If there were certain technical issues this time, I believe the experts can sort it out. And we will resolve this problem together with our partners.”

Mr. Zelensky said Western intelligence was critical. “This is what helps prevent killings when there is a warning about ballistic missiles,” he said in a social media post on Tuesday.

The cost of missing early warnings is perhaps felt most keenly in the eastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv, which lies only about 20 miles from the Russian border. Air-raid alerts sometimes cannot be sounded fast enough when Russia attacks the city.

On Monday night, volleys of drones hit Kharkiv, rocking the city center with loud, rumbling explosions. Fires burned in several locations. One strike tore into a residential building, collapsing apartments to the ground. The mayor, Ihor Terekhov, said in a social media post that four people had been killed on Monday and that two more strikes hit the city the next day.

On Tuesday, rescuers who worked through the night were still at the site of the residential building, pulling a body from the wreckage. Exhausted firefighters rested on the open trunks of vehicles as bulldozers cleared blackened rubble of bricks and belongings. A burning smell hung in the air.

Lyubov Smal, 69, one of the residents, with stitches on cuts to her face, said she had been cooking cutlets in her kitchen when a drone struck the building.

Bleeding, she made her way through smoke to the landing and was helped out by firefighters. Twelve hours later, she came back to plead for help in finding her cat. Resting from working through the night, two rescuers jumped up and climbed the blackened stairs to a third-floor apartment.

“He won’t bite us?” they jokingly asked. Minutes later, they were back with a big gray cat with yellow eyes. He dug his claws into the fleece of a neighbor, jumping at loud noises as bulldozers resumed clearing rubble.

Kamila Hrabchuk contributed reporting from Kharkiv.

item.title: Saudi Energy Giant Struck as War Spikes Between Houthis and Saudi Arabia
item.description:
A building owned by the energy giant Aramco was set ablaze late Tuesday in a strike on the Saudi city housing its headquarters, the kingdom’s energy ministry said, as war spiked between the Houthi militia in Yemen and Saudi Arabia.

The Houthis had threatened earlier in the day to attack the Aramco headquarters in the eastern city of Dhahran, but did not immediately take responsibility for the strike. It came after the Iranian-backed militia reported that two major oil facilities in Yemen had been attacked by Saudi forces on Tuesday.

The Saudi energy ministry said in a statement that the strike in Dhahran had hit an Aramco administrative building and caused “a limited fire” and no injuries.

By late Tuesday, residents of both countries were on edge as explosions were repeatedly heard in their capital cities. A Saudi-led coalition said it was targeting Yemeni facilities that support the Houthi war effort, while the Houthis vowed to retaliate against comparable sites in Saudi Arabia.

The Saudi authorities issued warnings of an aerial threat in the Saudi capital, Riyadh. And Maj. Gen. Turki al-Maliki, a spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition, said four cruise missiles fired toward Riyadh and southern Saudi Arabia had been intercepted, along with two drones.

Mr. al-Maliki also reported that a ballistic missile launched toward the city of Damman in the eastern part of the kingdom by the Houthis had been intercepted, and that shrapnel fell in a residential area of neighboring Dhahran.

The Houthis have struck Aramco’s facilities before and have frequently hit Saudi oil tankers in the Red Sea since tensions escalated between the two sides in July.

Yahya Saree, a military spokesman for the Houthis, had warned in a post on social media that, if Saudi forces were to attack Yemeni oil facilities, the militia would retaliate against Aramco’s headquarters, the company’s refinery in Riyadh and King Khalid International Airport, also in Riyadh.

The Houthis’ threat against Aramco came soon after Mr. al-Maliki urged civilians in Yemen to evacuate the vicinity of the al-Sabaha Central Station in Sanaa. Later on Tuesday, the Houthi-run television network al-Masirah reported that a Saudi airstrike had targeted that oil site.

Saudi strikes on the other oil facility, in port city of Hodeidah, killed at least two people, Anis al-Asbahi, a spokesman for the Houthi-run health ministry, said on Tuesday.

Shortly after the two oil facilities were reportedly struck, the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis in Yemen said it had targeted the Houthis’ military capabilities. In recent days, Houthi attacks have rocked Saudi Arabia, inflicting one of the highest death tolls there in years.

While the Saudis said they were “neutralizing the capabilities” of the militia, they did not confirm their targets. The coalition said in a statement that one oil complex in Sanaa, the Yemeni capital, and another in Hodeidah,were examples of civilian infrastructure that the Houthis were using to support their war effort.

Saudi warplanes have been bombing Houthi positions in Yemen in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, which is fighting to retake territory seized by the Houthis last month.

Over the weekend, the Houthis carried out the deadliest attack on the kingdom in more than a decade, striking King Khalid International Airport and killing at least 13 people. More than 300 people were wounded in the Saturday attack, the Saudi authorities said.

On Tuesday, Saudi officials, during a cabinet meeting led by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, vowed that the Houthis would bear the consequences for the “heinous attacks” on the kingdom’s airport.

The Houthis on Sunday accused Saudi Arabia of bombing an airport in the Yemeni capital, according to statements carried by the Saba news agency, which is run by the militia. The Saudi authorities have not commented on that assertion.

President Trump, in a social media post after the exchange of threats on Tuesday, wrote that the “Houthis are behaving very badly.” He said that he thought the militia had “learned their lesson a year ago when we bombed the HELL out of them.”

Though Mr. Trump condemned the Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia over the weekend, he has so far rebuffed the kingdom’s requests for U.S. support in the fight.

The Houthi militia has been fighting the internationally recognized, Saudi-backed government in Yemen since 2014. Saudi Arabia pledged to restore the government, declaring war on the Houthis and initiating a bombing campaign that set off one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises. A fragile truce agreed to in 2022 has unraveled in recent months.

Emboldened by regional instability, the battle-hardened Houthis have far less to lose against their more powerful, wealthier enemies, even as they imperil Saudi Arabia’s ambitions to transform itself into a global hub of business and tourism.

The Red Cross called for the urgent de-escalation of the conflict on Tuesday, warning that further escalation would be disastrous for tens of millions of civilians. “Civilians are paying an unacceptable price as a result of military operations in the Middle East,” said Mirjana Spoljaric, the president of the International Committee of the Red Cross.

Shuaib Almosawa contributed reporting from Sanaa, Yemen.

item.title: Trump Hands Victories to Putin, Who Offers More War in Return
item.description:
The wins for President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia came in rapid succession from Washington.

President Trump proffered sanctions relief for Russian diesel fuel. He publicly called for Ukraine to get a new leader. And he pressured Kyiv to stop a strike campaign against Russian oil facilities that has damaged the Russian economy.

Mr. Putin, in return, offered more war.

Minutes after Mr. Trump announced the diesel deal, the Kremlin reiterated Mr. Putin’s stance that he would not negotiate with Ukraine at the moment, because he remained angry about Ukrainian strikes during last month’s Russian parliamentary election.

The next day, Russia launched an attack on the Ukrainian city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 22 people, including four children. It was the latest in a near daily drumbeat of devastating Russian strikes, which have dramatically increased the civilian toll in Ukraine as Kyiv sorely lacks air-defense missiles.

And Mr. Putin has signaled that he plans to escalate further, aiming to knock out Ukraine’s power and water infrastructure in what Ukrainians expect to be the worst winter of the war.

Mr. Putin is reaping his victories as Mr. Trump’s own domestic political needs align with his longstanding inclination to tip the scales toward Russia. With the American president focused on trying to bring down fuel prices before a difficult midterm election, he is pushing Kyiv to trade away its leverage for nothing in return.

Ukraine has said it would suspend its oil refinery strikes if Russia ceased attacks on Ukrainian energy facilities heading into the winter. But when Mr. Trump announced an “energy cease-fire” on Sunday, he meant only a suspension of oil refinery strikes in both countries, The New York Times reported. Ukraine has only one major oil refinery, and Russian strikes took it largely out of service in 2022.

Mr. Trump has promoted his energy deal with Mr. Putin as an example of how he is tackling America’s diesel challenge, which experts say is more attributable to the war with Iran. But it was seen as a betrayal by Ukrainian officials, undercutting years of Western efforts to starve the Russian war machine of cash.

It may not even do much to lower diesel prices. Economists have said the amount of fuel discussed is not enough to move the needle significantly.

“The U.S. president is focused on one thing, which is himself and his reading of the world,” said Alexander Gabuev, director of the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center.

That reading, Mr. Gabuev said, includes Mr. Trump’s stubborn denial that his own decision to go to war against Iran caused fuel prices to skyrocket. “In his picture of the world, the Gulf war doesn’t play a role in the current diesel crisis, and there needs to be a magical solution with someone he is predisposed to, who is Vladimir Putin.”

Earlier this year, things were looking difficult for Mr. Putin. Expenditures on the war were rapidly expanding. Progress on the battlefield had slowed to a crawl. Global prices for oil, Russia’s top export, had slumped to around $60 a barrel.

Then Mr. Trump launched the war in Iran, alongside Israel. Oil prices jumped to over $100 a barrel. The vast use of air defense missiles by the United States and its Gulf allies in response to Iran’s attacks dried up the supply for Ukraine, leaving it increasingly vulnerable. With Mr. Trump looking for a way out, Russia’s longstanding relationship with Iran offered Mr. Putin a new calling card with Washington.

As the Iran war accorded benefits to Russia, Ukraine tried to limit Moscow’s economic gains with increasingly effective strikes on oil refineries — the campaign that Mr. Trump is now demanding that Kyiv end.

Kyiv’s systematic targeting of Russian oil infrastructure brought the war home to Russia as never before, causing lines at the pump across the country and forcing Russia, one of the world’s largest diesel suppliers, to suspend exports.

As Ukrainian strikes decreased production, Russia’s tax revenue from oil and gas for the first three quarters of the year fell by 17 percent compared with the same period in 2025, even as fuel prices rose dramatically. (A rise in the ruble and Russian domestic fuel subsidies also played a role.)

Now, the diesel deal could pour billions of dollars into the Russian economy. An extended suspension of Ukrainian strikes on oil refineries, if Kyiv agrees to one under the intense American pressure, could generate much more money.

The wins for Mr. Putin go beyond the diesel deal. Mr. Trump has also welcomed Russian ministers this year for Group of 20 events in North Carolina and Wisconsin, and he plans to host Mr. Putin in December at the G-20 summit in Miami. His administration is also negotiating potential business deals with the Kremlin, in what Mr. Trump’s team has cast as inducements to a peace deal.

The Russians want even more from the U.S. president, analysts say.

When Mr. Trump returned to office in 2025, Moscow hoped that the United States would cut off all support for Ukraine and force President Volodymyr Zelensky into a capitulation largely on the Kremlin’s terms.

Mr. Trump’s Oval Office blowup with Mr. Zelensky in March of last year made it seem as if Moscow’s dream was within reach. The Trump administration’s decision to halt weapons donations to Ukraine and suspend intelligence sharing stoked hopes even further.

But in the months since, U.S. intelligence sharing resumed. Mr. Trump brokered a deal for the Europeans to buy weapons from the United States for Ukraine. And U.S.-led peace negotiations fizzled as the Trump administration became distracted by the war in Iran.

Fyodor Lukyanov, a Russian political scientist who advises the Kremlin, wrote last month that Ukraine would be left with little defense if the United States completely ceased its military support.

“But Trump is unlikely to take that step,” Mr. Lukyanov wrote, “even if he were personally inclined to do so,” because a complete Ukrainian defeat would not win him any plaudits in the American political establishment.

Such a move by Mr. Trump might also invite more aggressive actions from Congress, particularly after the midterms. The Senate recently passed a Russia sanctions bill, named in honor of Senator Lindsey Graham of South Carolina, with a veto-proof margin, though Mr. Trump retains the power to waive its provisions on national security grounds and will need to do so to import Russian diesel.

As Mr. Trump so far stops short of forcing Ukraine into a surrender, Mr. Putin is likely to continue his escalation, said Hanna Notte, an analyst at the James Martin Center for Nonproliferation Studies and the author of a new book on Russian foreign policy called “We Will Outlast Them.”

She said of Mr. Putin, “It’s quite clear that his intention right now is to inflict a really, really nasty winter on the Ukrainians.”

Although Russian forces remain largely stuck on the battlefield, Mr. Putin has long believed that he can achieve victory in Ukraine by outlasting Kyiv and what he sees as its fickle Western allies, analysts say. He believes they will eventually pull back their extensive support of Ukraine as their own domestic problems mount, analysts say.

The French presidential election next year could usher in the far-right leader Marine Le Pen, who has advocated halting financial assistance to Ukraine. Chancellor Friedrich Merz of Germany is also under pressure from a surging far-right party that has pressed for ending support for Ukraine. And both Britain and France are struggling under huge government debts that are far more expensive to service at current interest rates.

“You could make the case that from the Kremlin’s perspective, the future looks better, more conducive to an outcome of the war that is closer to their terms,” said Sam Charap, a Russia analyst at the RAND Corporation. “You have to change that perception of the future, diminish that optimism, to affect their calculus.”

item.title: Trump Squeezes Ukraine, Again
item.description:
I’m in France this week at a gathering with journalists from around the world to debate the future of our profession. There are some incredibly brave people here, reporting from the front lines of conflicts we often cover in this newsletter. More on that later.

For now, speaking of conflicts: Last week, President Trump bypassed America’s own sanctions on buying Russian energy and cut a deal to, well, buy Russian energy. That means one NATO member may soon be helping to fund not just Russia’s war on Ukraine, but also its ongoing hybrid warfare against other NATO members. Today, I’m handing the mic over to my editor, Alicia Wittmeyer, who is writing about what Trump’s diesel deal means for Ukraine, and for Europe.

By Alicia P.Q. Wittmeyer

It had already been a terrible week in Ukraine.

Last Wednesday, Russia hit an apartment building in the town of Pryluky in northern Ukraine, hundreds of kilometers away from any combat zone. The strike killed 22 people, including five children.

On Thursday, Russia struck a bus in the town of Kramatorsk, killing 33 on their commute.

On Friday came the surprise. Trump announced he had reached a deal with President Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel fuel into the United States. The agreement undermines years of efforts by the West to deprive the Russian state of funding for its war efforts. If it goes ahead, the exchange could send some $4 billion of American money into the Russian economy, energy experts estimate. Our Moscow bureau chief, Paul Sonne, writes about why this has been a gift to Putin.

Trump’s announcement was followed, on Saturday, by a new Russian attack. This time it was on the city of Zaporizhzhia — 22 dead, including four children.

For Ukraine, the deal comes at a particularly bad time.

Russia, as it does every winter, is stepping up efforts to target Ukraine’s civilian infrastructure, including, crucially, its energy infrastructure — part of an ongoing effort to both cripple Ukraine’s economy and break its will to fight. This coming winter might be the hardest yet. Ukraine is facing a critical shortage of air defenses; Russia is equipped with new, deadlier weapons.

For Ukraine, the problem with Trump’s deal is not just the money, my colleagues in Ukraine tell me. We still don’t know whether the deal will go through, and if it does, how much money the Russian government will actually collect.

The bigger problem is that Moscow is engaged in an “unrelenting campaign to make Ukraine’s towns and cities unlivable,” as one of our Ukraine correspondents, Marc Santora, recently put it. And in the aftermath of the deal announcement, Trump is pressuring Ukraine to give up the best tool it has for fighting back.

A lopsided “ENERGY CEASEFIRE”

Remember the dramatic video from this summer of the roof of an oil storage facility on the outskirts of Moscow flying into the air on a plume of black smoke, before plummeting down to earth? That was the result of a Ukrainian attack on a Russian oil refinery.

I spoke to my colleague Constant Méheut, who is based in Kyiv and has been covering the economic side of this war. He told me about how good Ukraine has gotten at hitting Russian refineries, and how important that’s become to the country’s war efforts.

Ukraine has targeted Russia’s oil infrastructure since early 2024, but in the last year and a half, it’s become incredibly effective. According to the International Energy Agency, in the first eight months of 2026, a Russian refinery was hit on average once every three days.

The attacks have taken a toll. Russia’s reported gas output is down by 20 percent compared with 2025 levels; diesel production has fallen by nearly 30 percent — all of which means less money for the fight.

Now, Trump wants Ukraine to stop. The day after he announced the deal with Russia, he accused Kyiv of causing a “world problem” with the attacks, blaming it for high diesel prices in the U.S. (Most energy analysts see the high prices as primarily driven by the war in Iran, with Russia’s decreased capacity an aggravating factor.)

On Sunday, Trump announced — seemingly unilaterally — an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE.” It wasn’t clear what he meant; neither Ukraine nor Russia confirmed they’d agreed to anything. But a person familiar with Trump’s thinking told my colleagues that by “energy cease-fire,” Trump meant only an end to refinery attacks.

Ukraine effectively has no operational oil refineries — meaning this cease-fire, such as it is, would really only tie the hands of one party. As if to underscore the point, shortly after the announcement, Russia struck a power plant in eastern Ukraine.

A stepped-up hybrid war campaign

The diesel announcement follows a pattern that’s become familiar over the course of Trump’s second term. The administration does something that undermines Ukraine; European leaders — many of whom see Ukraine’s fight as partly their own — are left stunned and at a loss for how to respond.

If the deal comes at a bad time for Ukraine, it also comes at a bad time for Europe. The continent has worked since the start of the war to reduce its own consumption of Russian energy, but has not eliminated it completely, even as Russia has grown increasingly aggressive in its hybrid war efforts on the continent. Yesterday, the prime minister of Bulgaria, a NATO member, said drones had struck two ships off the country’s Black Sea coast. He pointed the finger at Russia, which has targeted the area in an effort to cut off Ukrainian seaborne grain exports.

The world now waits to see what comes next — whether Ukraine will really stop attacking Russian oil refineries and, if it doesn’t, whether the U.S. will really cut off intelligence sharing, as it’s threatened to.

On Monday, though, Europe’s leaders witnessed the strange sight of NATO’s top military commander, a member of the U.S. Air Force, giving a speech in which he sought to reassure members that NATO had a plan for deterring Russia. They watched him with the knowledge that NATO’s most important member could, very soon, be helping fund the Russian war machine.

Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer after surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung, the Vatican said.

Kimberly Guilfoyle resigned as the U.S. ambassador to Greece after the White House asked her to do so. She’s facing accusations that she asked a donor to pay off her credit card bill.

The head of MI5, Britain’s domestic security agency, warned of threats from Iran and said Russia “remains aggressor No. 1.”

The Iran-backed Houthi militia threatened to strike facilities belonging to Saudi Arabia’s oil giant Aramco as both sides trade threats.

A cyberattack hit refrigeration systems in more than 400 supermarkets in France.

Russia detained a Japanese journalist on suspicion of espionage.

Technology stocks around the world tumbled, with losses concentrated in the chip-making sector.

After nearly a decade in power, President Emmanuel Macron has failed to solve the manifold problems afflicting France’s economy — problems he had promised to address, our Paris bureau chief, Mark Landler, writes.

A Times investigation has found that violent threats have become a new normal among American elected officials. My colleague Nick Corasaniti interviewed some of them about living under the threat of political violence. Watch the video.

A judge in Las Vegas sentenced a man to 40 years to life in prison for orchestrating the murder of Tupac Shakur in a 1996 drive-by shooting.

Apple introduced a new home smart device, HomeView, which will be available in eight countries, including Britain and India.

The Haitian Canadian author Thélyson Orélien admitted to plagiarism but denied using A.I. to write parts of his book.

The most clicked link in your newsletter yesterday was about a Norwegian adventurer’s wilderness trek in Canada.

Football: About a year before the World Cup, FIFA signed a $4 million lease in Trump Tower. The office is mostly empty.

Formula 1: A track built on the outskirts of Kigali, Rwanda’s capital, will host the new African Grand Prix.

In a half-billion years or so, we might have to move. That’s because our sun will start to swell, making Earth too hot to sustain complex life. But scientists say there are superhabitable planets outside our solar system where carbon-based life could persist and perhaps become even more diverse than it is now.

Germany is the birthplace of the automobile. It’s the home of Volkswagen, BMW and Mercedes-Benz. These days, it’s also a top destination for Chinese companies selling cheaper cars.

Shut out of the U.S. by tariffs, Chinese automakers are focusing on Europe. BYD, the dominant Chinese maker of electric vehicles, wants everyone in Germany to be within 20 minutes of a showroom. That doesn’t sit well with some in Europe. Read more about Europe’s love-hate relationship with Chinese cars.

Like many British seaside destinations, the Welsh town of Porthcawl offers surfing, fish and chips, and an amusement park. But it is perhaps best known for something decidedly American: Every September, it hosts one of the world’s largest gatherings of Elvis tribute artists and fans.

The festival draws about 40,000 each year, more than doubling the town’s population for a weekend. “You couldn’t think of a more inappropriate place to put an Elvis festival,” the organizer said. “But it seems to work.” Take a look.

When you think of Wales, your head probably doesn’t fill with images of celebrities. But the country has produced lots of them. Which star below is NOT from Wales? Click to see if you’re correct.

Anthony Hopkins

Tom Jones

Gwyneth Paltrow

Catherine Zeta-Jones

This pasta with fish ragù can take you straight to Sicily, no passport needed. The roasted fish pieces tossed with a sauce of sweet peppers, a splash of white wine and a bit of tomato is reminiscent of a meaty Bolognese, but lighter and fresher.

Watch: Aaron Sorkin’s new movie is about how social media platforms have rewired our brains.

Restore: Damaged wooden floors can be touched up with only a few tools and materials.

Read: In a startling exposé, two journalists make the case that the Havana Syndrome is real.

Loosen up: Sitting all day? These moves can help prevent aches and pains.

Here are today’s Spelling Bee, Mini Crossword, Wordle and Sudoku. Find all our games here.

That’s it for today. See you tomorrow! — Katrin

Alicia P.Q. Wittmeyer was our guest writer today.

We welcome your feedback. Send us your suggestions at theworld@nytimes.com.

item.title: Leo XIV’s Cancer Diagnosis Tests the Assumption of a Long Papacy
item.description:
When Leo XIV was elected pope less than 18 months ago, he seemed to have years ahead of him to shape the Roman Catholic church. At 69, he was young by recent papal standards, and the faithful marveled at his energy and apparently robust health. He was known to play tennis regularly and had no reported medical problems. He reintroduced summer vacations to make sure he remained fresh and rested.

Leo, the first pope born in the United States, marked a break from his predecessor, Francis, who started his papacy at age 76 but had already had a lung condition at a young age. A year into his papacy, Francis told reporters that he thought he would serve as pope for only two or three years before going “off to the house of the Father.” Francis lasted a dozen years, but toward the end of his papacy had a bad knee, intestinal problems and finally, pneumonia in both lungs.

Now, Leo, who was diagnosed with lung cancer on Tuesday, suddenly faces the same sense of urgency and questions of longevity that had hung over Francis.

The diagnosis poses a lurching shift in the outlook for a pope whose relative youth and health indicated he had decades to reign. It casts uncertainty over his travel schedule, his agenda and his efforts to unite the Church. And in the worst-case scenario, it raises questions about succession that most thought would not have to be addressed for years to come.

“The common consensus was he’s young, we’re in for a long papacy,” said Christopher White, a senior fellow at the Initiative on Catholic Social Thought and Public Life at Georgetown University and the author of “Pope Leo XIV: Inside the Conclave and the Dawn of a New Papacy.”

While Leo was not as young as Pope John Paul II, who was just 58 when he was elected in 1978, Leo’s apparent healthy lifestyle added to an impression of his vitality. “Leo has the profile of someone who takes care of himself,” Mr. White said. “So that has added to the shock.”

At his weekly general audiences in St. Peter’s Square or on international journeys, he showed no signs of impaired health and kept a hectic schedule. In Rome, his agenda was packed with meetings and over the summer he released a major document on artificial intelligence.

From the beginning of his papacy Leo, born Robert Francis Prevost in Chicago, behaved like someone who believed he could take his time. In the early months, he was considered slow to act. He made few personnel changes and did not immediately grab headlines with dramatic pronouncements or policy moves. He seemed more interested in soothing tensions and listening.

And even when Leo became more strident, as when he criticized the Trump administration’s war in Iran, he responded only when the president specifically attacked him, and then retreated, saying he did not want a fight. With his quiet, steady demeanor, he gave the sense that he was in no rush.

After Francis’s tumultuous papacy, during which conservative Christians balked at the progressive Catholicism he elevated, Leo was seen as a leader who could calm the Church. Leo has been popular not only with both progressive and conservative Catholics, but with people outside the faith who see him as a moral leader in troubled times.

His illness will inevitably unsettle the Church, particularly depending on how transparent the Vatican continues to be about the pope’s progress through treatment. “This kind of thing just creates disquiet,” said David Gibson, director of the Center on Religion and Culture at Fordham University.

For now, the pope, who recently traveled to Spain and France, has said he will keep to his plan to travel to Latin America in November. Inevitably, any changes to his schedule will be scrutinized closely.

The pope’s doctors announced that the surgery to remove a lower lobe of his right lung was successful and had no complications. Information released by the Vatican suggested the cancer was caught at an early stage.

If Leo makes a strong recovery, Mr. Gibson said, the cancer could become part of a heroic narrative that buoys Leo’s reputation. Pope John Paul II, who started out in excellent health, was seriously wounded by an assassination attempt in 1981 and spent three months in the hospital. His recovery became part of “the mythology that grew up around him,” said Mr. Gibson.

And while few people survive assassination attempts, many people live with cancer. Pope Leo’s illness and how he behaves during treatment could serve as an inspiration to others suffering from disease.

“There’s also an opportunity for him in this vulnerability to be as great a comfort to many people as he was in the first year and a half of his papacy,” Mr. Gibson said.

item.title: Pope Leo’s Cancer Surgery Draws Outpouring From World Leaders
item.description:
Political and religious leaders responded with prayers and messages of support after the Vatican’s announcement on Tuesday that Pope Leo XIV had undergone surgery for lung cancer.

The U.N. secretary general, António Guterres, wished the pope a speedy recovery and said on social media that his thoughts and prayers were with him and “the Catholic community worldwide.”

The Vatican said the 90-minute procedure had successfully removed part of the pope’s right lung. The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, a Catholic, said his thoughts and prayers were with the spiritual leader as he recovers.

“Pope Leo XIV is a source of inspiration to Catholics right around the world,” Mr. Albanese wrote on social media. “He is a voice for peace, humanity and reason in our modern world.”

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also Catholic, said that he and his wife were praying for the pope. “May the Lord give him strength and the Holy Spirit guide the medical professionals taking care of the Holy Father,” he wrote.

Some said the pope’s illness should be a reminder to pray for others who have cancer or to get screenings themselves. The United States Conference of Catholic Bishops urged people to pray not only for the pope but also for his caregivers.

“We ask the faithful to continue praying for Pope Leo’s recovery and for the doctors and staff caring for him,” the group wrote. “We also hold in prayer all who are living with cancer, their families, and those who care for them.”

Ronald A. Hicks, who was named archbishop of New York by Pope Leo, wished the pontiff well on behalf of the archdiocese, the country and the world. His counterpart in San Francisco, Salvatore J. Cordileone, gave thanks for the pope’s successful surgery and urged people to join him in praying for the patient and his medical team “as they discern the next steps in his treatment.”

Alexander Sample, the archbishop of Portland, Ore., asked Catholics and “all people of good will” to pray for the pope’s recovery.

“At a time when war, division and uncertainty weigh heavily on people around the world, the Holy Father’s calls for peace, dialogue and respect for the dignity of every person offer a much-needed message of hope to people everywhere,” he wrote.

Pope Leo’s plight was also addressed by a lawmaker from his home state of Illinois.

Calling the pontiff “one of our own,” Representative Jonathan L. Jackson, Democrat of Illinois, wrote that the Catholic leader was “a Chicago kid who carried the values of our neighborhoods all the way onto the world stage,” and that the whole city was with him now and wished him strength and a full recovery.

Mr. Jackson also urged people to talk to their doctors, in light of the pope’s lung cancer diagnosis, noting that “catching it early saves lives.”

Anthony Scaramucci, a podcaster and former White House communications director for President Trump, kept his message short: “We pray for the Holy Father today and everyday.”

item.title: Turkey Raids Pro-Opposition TV Station
item.description:
The police raided the headquarters of Turkey’s most widely watched opposition news channel on Wednesday and a court appointed a government administrator to run it, the latest in a series of legal moves by the government of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan against political rivals.

The channel, Halk TV, switched at 6:30 a.m. local time from its normal live newscast to archival content. It announced on its website that “hundreds of police” had come into its offices and were barring people from entering.

The Istanbul Chief Prosecutor’s Office said the raid was part of an investigation into the channel’s chairman, Cafer Mahiroglu, on suspicion of bribery, bid rigging and money laundering. It ordered the detention of 17 people, 11 of whom had already been arrested.

Mr. Mahiroglu was ordered detained but he is outside Turkey. He has denied all charges.

The government’s seizure of Halk TV, the country’s last mainstream news channel critical of Mr. Erdogan, elevated concerns about press freedom in Turkey and prompted new accusations that the government was using the law to weaken its political opposition.

“A dawn raid on a television channel, appointing a trustee — only dictators would do such a thing,” Ozgur Ozel, the head of Turkey’s largest opposition party, wrote on social media.

He accused the government of appointing administrators, known as “trustees,” to run companies, municipalities and television stations as a way to “trample the people’s will” amid widespread concern over Turkey’s economic situation.

Halk TV is the fifth major Turkish news outlet to have its leadership replaced by the government. The station provided continuous coverage of local and international news but with a clear orientation toward the political opposition, whose speeches, rallies and meetings other channels ignore.

During the last two years, the government has launched a vast series of legal moves against Mr. Erdogan’s political foes. Scores of opposition party figures, including mayors, have been arrested, mostly on corruption-related charges.

The crackdown has altered Turkey’s political map. A court ruling caused the country’s largest opposition party to split in two, dividing Mr. Erdogan’s foes. Some opposition mayors have been removed from office and replaced by members of Mr. Erdogan’s governing Justice and Development Party.

Last week, the mayor of Izmir, Turkey’s third largest city and a historic opposition bastion, defected from the opposition to Mr. Erdogan’s party.

The government says its legal system is free from political interference. Mr. Erdogan has characterized the opposition as deeply corrupt, comparing the spread of what he has characterized as its schemes to “the arms of an octopus.”

In an interview, Bahadır Ozgur, an investigative columnist and correspondent at Halk TV, said the police had arrived before dawn on Wednesday, blocked access to the street and searched the headquarters.

No journalists remain in the channel’s control room, he said, and its social media accounts were all now controlled by the government-appointed overseer.

He said the seizure of the channel was part of a broad effort by the government to “incapacitate all of the opposition’s means” since it won local elections in many of Turkey’s largest cities in 2024.

“It was Halk TV’s turn as the most effective media outlet of the opposition,” Mr. Ozgur said.

Mr. Mahiroglu, the chairman of the channel, said in a video posted on social media that seven members of his family had been arrested, including his 70-year-old brother.

“Today is a dark day for Turkey,” he said. “People’s right to receive news is being prevented, with political aims.”

The end of Halk TV’s live newscast came hours before a top opposition politician, Ekrem Imamoglu, was expected to present his defense in court against charges that he ran a criminal organization inside Istanbul’s City Hall while serving as mayor between 2019 and 2025.

The channel was expected to cover the defense, while Turkey’s government-aligned channels have largely ignored the trial.

Mr. Imamoglu, who was arrested last year after announcing that he planned to challenge Mr. Erdogan in Turkey’s next presidential election, has dismissed the charges against him as politically motivated. He recently intended to publish a book to make his case directly to Turkish voters, but it was banned just days before it was to hit the shelves.

Turkey rated 163rd out of 180 countries on Reporters Without Borders’ 2026 World Press Freedom Index.

“Authoritarianism is gaining ground in Turkey and media pluralism is being called into question,” the organization wrote. “All possible means are used to undermine critics.”
